keyVerseText: And Lamech said unto his wives, Adah and Zillah, Hear my voice; ye wives of Lamech, hearken unto my speech: for I have slain a man to my wounding, and a young man to my hurt. I have: or, I would slay a man in my wound, etc to my hurt: or, in my hurt
rootMeaning: The Hebrew noun אִמְרָה (ʼimrâh) is the feminine form of אֵמֶר (ʼêmer), both rooted in the concept of speech or something said. While its common English glosses include 'word' or 'speech,' the root conveys a sense of an utterance appointed or commanded, emphasizing not just casual words but purposeful, authoritative communication. This etymology highlights that אִמְרָה carries the weight of a declared message, often with divine or legal significance.
usageInScripture: Across its 37 occurrences, אִמְרָה is translated variously as 'thy word,' 'the word,' or 'my speech,' indicating both personal and divine communications. The consistent use of the term to denote authoritative speech, including the 'word of God' or the Torah, reveals its role as a vehicle for commands and promises. This range of translations underscores the term's flexibility yet maintains its core identity as a meaningful, impactful utterance.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding אִמְרָה as a divinely appointed utterance enriches our grasp of Scripture as God's authoritative communication to humanity. It reminds believers that the words of the Bible are not mere human expressions but carry the weight of God's command and promise. This insight affirms the trustworthiness and power of God's word in shaping faith and life. Recognizing the term's root meaning helps Christians appreciate the Bible as living speech that calls for response and obedience, reflecting the personal and sovereign nature of God.
keyVerseReflection: In Genesis 4:23, Lamech's call to 'hearken unto my speech' (אִמְרָה) underscores the seriousness of his words as a deliberate and authoritative utterance. The use of אִמְרָה here conveys that his speech is not casual but a significant declaration, emphasizing the weight and intent behind his confession of violence. This highlights the power of spoken words to convey identity and intent, reflecting the broader biblical theme of speech as an expression of the heart and will.
